title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Water-utility attacks widen to 7 states — Georgia joins Michigan and Minnesota as the FBI probes an Iran-tied crew and operators fall back to manual control
items.content_text: The coordinated campaign against internet-facing water and wastewater PLCs keeps spreading. On 3 August Georgia became the latest state to confirm intrusions, joining Michigan (nine systems, 1 Aug) and Minnesota, where the state confirmed 30-plus community systems were struck 26–27 July — briefly forcing Braham and others to run controls manually. The FBI and EPA now count at least seven states hit since 27 July. Attackers changed device IPs and passwords to lock operators out; some sites saw pressure drops and localized flooding, though officials stress drinking water stayed safe. The FBI flags Rockwell/Allen-Bradley MicroLogix PLCs; researchers cite CyberAv3ngers hallmarks and KEV-listed CVE-2021-22681. Iran is the leading suspect, but no forensic link is confirmed — investigators are still weighing a false flag, and President Trump publicly disputed the Iran attribution.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: FBI/EPA alert & MNIT / Michigan / Georgia / city statements (Braham, South St. Paul, Plymouth, Maple Plain); Tenable assessment — via SecurityWeek, The Register, The Hacker News, CNN, NBC News, Washington Post & MPR
_otthreatfeed.date_note: 26–27 Jul incident — MN confirmed 28 Jul; FBI/EPA 7 states 30–31 Jul; Michigan 1 Aug; Georgia joined 3 Aug 2026

items.title: Coca-Cola confirms Fairlife data was stolen as production restarts after ransomware stop
items.content_text: Coca-Cola said on 27 July that its Fairlife dairy subsidiary has resumed the majority of production at all four of its US plants, roughly ten days after a ransomware event forced a full production suspension first disclosed in a 16 July SEC 8-K. The company says retail availability was largely cushioned by existing inventory and that product quality and safety were never affected. The extortion side then escalated: the Anubis ransomware group had listed Coca-Cola/Fairlife on its leak site on 20 July, claiming about 1 TB of stolen data and encryption of Nutanix infrastructure, and on 28 July Coca-Cola confirmed that data was in fact taken in the attack after its 27 July ransom deadline lapsed. For OT defenders the lesson stands even as lines restart: ransomware in the plant IT and production-scheduling layer can halt a food & beverage operation without ever touching a controller.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Coca-Cola statement & press release / SEC 8-K / Anubis leak-site claim — via Just Food, Reuters & SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Disclosed 16 Jul — production resumed 27 Jul, data theft confirmed 28 Jul 2026

items.title: NSA, CISA, FBI and 12 allied nations warn Russia’s FSB Center 16 is harvesting configs from critical-infrastructure routers
items.content_text: A joint advisory (AA26-194A, “Improve Router Hygiene”) attributes a long-running campaign to Russia’s FSB Center 16 — the actor also tracked as Berserk Bear / Dragonfly / Energetic Bear. The actors scan for internet-exposed networking devices running SNMP with default or weak community strings, then issue SNMP writes abusing the Cisco config-copy MIB to exfiltrate device configurations over TFTP; they also opportunistically exploit Cisco Smart Install and known device CVEs. Stolen configs expose network topology, credentials and VPN details — ideal reconnaissance for deeper access. Named sectors most at risk include Energy, Communications, Defense Industrial Base, Financial Services, Government (especially state/local) and Healthcare. For OT teams, the perimeter routers and firewalls fronting plant networks are exactly the under-audited devices in scope.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA AA26-194A / NSA / FBI — via Nextgov & Forbes

items.title: SonicWall SMA 1000 zero-days exploited in the wild — a favorite OT remote-access on-ramp under attack
items.content_text: SonicWall confirmed attackers are exploiting two zero-days in its SMA 1000 secure-access appliances: CVE-2026-15409, a critical (CVSS 10) server-side request forgery in the Work Place interface reachable by an unauthenticated remote attacker, and CVE-2026-15410 (CVSS 7.2), a post-authentication OS command-injection flaw in the management console. Rapid7’s MDR team observed the bugs used for stealthy initial access on internet-facing appliances — harvesting credentials, active session databases and TOTP MFA seeds — and Volexity has since tied the activity to a threat cluster it tracks as UTA0533. CISA added both to its KEV catalog on 14 July with a 17 July federal remediation deadline. SMA-class VPN/remote-access gateways are a common bridge into OT networks, and stolen sessions and MFA seeds are exactly what enables the credential-driven, living-off-the-land pivots defenders keep seeing.

items.title: Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator CVSS 10 zero-day exploited — SD-WAN control plane for remote and plant sites under attack
items.content_text: Arista and CISA confirmed active in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-16812, a maximum-severity (CVSS 10.0) unauthenticated OS command-injection flaw in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), the centralized platform used to configure and manage VeloCloud SD-WAN fabrics and their edge appliances. A remote attacker needs no credentials to reach privileged internal functions and run arbitrary commands on the orchestrator host — and Arista warns that compromising the VCO can extend attacker access to the managed VeloCloud Edge devices themselves. CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on 27 July with a 30 July federal remediation deadline. SD-WAN orchestrators frequently stitch together remote sites, substations and plant networks, so a compromised control plane is a direct route into the WAN paths that reach OT.

items.title: Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center hard-coded-password zero-day exploited — the box that controls plant-perimeter firewalls
items.content_text: Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-20316 on 29 July, a hard-coded-password flaw in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) that lets an unauthenticated attacker, on the network or the internet, log in to an affected instance with a low-privilege account and no valid credentials. The base CVSS is only 5.3, but Cisco assigned it a High security-impact rating because it can be chained to escalate privileges, and Cisco PSIRT confirmed it was exploited as a zero-day before a fix existed. CISA added it to the KEV catalog the same day. FMC is the central management plane for Cisco Secure Firewall deployments, including the firewalls that segment and front many OT networks — so a foothold here lets an attacker read the ruleset, weaken segmentation or map the environment before touching a controller.

items.title: Cl0p launches a large-scale extortion wave against PTC Windchill and FlexPLM — a manufacturing PLM backbone under active data theft
items.content_text: The Cl0p ransomware crew is running a broad data-theft campaign against internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM servers, exploiting the critical (CVSS 9.8) unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw CVE-2026-12569 — already in CISA’s KEV catalog — to drop JSP web shells and exfiltrate engineering data. Researchers at BleepingComputer and The Hacker News report Cl0p began mass extortion around 20 July, emailing large internal distribution lists with a “Windchill PDMLink module serious data leak” subject to pressure victims, with confirmed impact in manufacturing, automotive, aerospace and apparel. Windchill sits deep in engineering environments — holding CAD, BOM and process data and often bridging enterprise and plant networks — so a web shell here is a foothold with a clear line toward OT-adjacent assets. Cl0p has a long record of turning a single PLM/file-transfer flaw into a mass campaign, and this one is now moving fast.

items.title: Lantronix serial-to-IP converter flaw exploited — the warning about OT edge gear plays out
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2025-67038, a flaw in Lantronix EDS-series serial-to-IP converters, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 14 July after confirming active exploitation. The bug was originally disclosed in April through the BRIDGE:BREAK research into serial device servers. These converters bolt legacy serial field equipment onto IP networks — a fixture in water, energy and manufacturing plants — and often sit at the OT edge with little monitoring. The KEV listing confirms the pattern defenders keep seeing: adversaries reach for the cheap, forgotten boxes that bridge serial and IP long before they touch a PLC.

items.title: Manufacturing stays ransomware’s No. 1 target as new gangs emerge weekly
items.content_text: Black Kite’s 2026 Ransomware Report, out this week, counted 7,551 disclosed victims over the year to March 2026 — up nearly 25% — with disclosures accelerating about 60% in the second half. Manufacturing again topped every sector for the fourth straight year, with roughly 1,660 victims (about 22% of all disclosures), and 61 new ransomware brands appeared over the period, more than one a week. The finding OT teams should sit with: a rescan showed 30.8% of victims still carried a Known Exploited Vulnerability after their incident, meaning the exposure that let attackers in was never closed. Industrial operators remain the most-hit vertical and the slowest to remediate.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Black Kite 2026 Ransomware Report — via Help Net Security & Cybersecurity Dive

items.title: World Leaks dumps Reliance files tied to India’s largest nuclear plant
items.content_text: The extortion group World Leaks posted a large cache of files on its dark-web site that it attributed to India’s Reliance Group, including purported blueprints and supplier details connected to the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant. Reliance — a contractor building infrastructure for Kudankulam Units 3 and 4 — confirmed a “partial breach” of data held on a server run by third-party data-center provider Yotta and said it had informed the government. The roughly 19,000 most sensitive files reportedly include ventilation and cooling-system drawings and a control-room floor layout, but not the Russian-supplied reactor core systems. This is a supply-chain data exposure rather than an OT compromise — but leaked engineering detail on a nuclear site shows how contractor and third-party data becomes an OT risk of its own.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Reliance Group / Reuters — via Business Standard & Al Jazeera

items.title: Blackfield ransomware demands $2M from motor maker Nidec after breaching a Taiwanese subsidiary
items.content_text: The Blackfield ransomware crew has listed Nidec — the large Japanese electric-motor and industrial-component manufacturer — on its leak site, demanding $2 million and claiming it stole more than two terabytes of data from subsidiary Nidec Chaun-Choung Technology in Taiwan. The group says the archive spans employee, financial, procurement, manufacturing, legal and IT records, and is offering to sell or publish it if unpaid. Nidec states the subsidiary runs on an independent network that limited the intrusion’s reach and has not confirmed the volume or contents of any stolen files — the figures come from the attacker, which has every incentive to inflate them. No production impact has been reported, but it is another reminder that manufacturing remains the most-targeted sector for industrial ransomware.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Blackfield leak-site claim / Nidec — via BleepingComputer

items.title: Swiss train maker Stadler Rail refuses $12.3M ransom after a supplier data-exchange breach
items.content_text: Stadler Rail confirmed the Everest extortion group stole technical data after compromising credentials for a data-exchange platform the manufacturer shares with one of its suppliers. Stadler says its own IT systems, production lines and in-service rail vehicles worldwide were not affected, that the stolen files are technical material with no bearing on railway safety, and that it will not pay — publicly stating it is “not susceptible to extortion” and filing a criminal complaint with Thurgau police. Everest, a group that shifted from encryption to pure data-theft extortion, is demanding roughly $12.3 million (CHF 10 million). For OT defenders in transit and manufacturing this is the recurring supply-chain pattern: the breach landed on a shared third-party platform, not the target’s plant, yet exposed sensitive engineering data all the same.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Stadler Rail statement / Everest leak-site claim — via BleepingComputer, The Register & Railway Gazette

items.title: CISA re-issues Iranian PLC-attack advisory (AA26-097A) — CyberAv3ngers now confirmed hitting Rockwell, Schneider and Siemens controllers
items.content_text: CISA, FBI, NSA, EPA, DOE and Cyber Command updated advisory AA26-097A on 22 July, broadening the campaign that Iran’s IRGC-linked CyberAv3ngers persona has run against internet-exposed programmable logic controllers across US critical infrastructure. The update documents project-file exfiltration for the first time, adds detection guidance for malicious changes to reusable code modules inside Rockwell Automation PLC programs, and expands confirmed targeting to Schneider Electric and Siemens controllers — with actors abusing the vendors’ own engineering software (Studio 5000, EcoStruxure Control Expert, TIA Portal) to reach exposed PLCs. Agencies say victims in water/wastewater, energy and government have already suffered operational disruption and financial loss after actors manipulated PLC logic and altered HMI/SCADA readings. This is the agency-level framing behind this week’s Minnesota water incident (see top story): confirmed hands-on manipulation of control logic, not reconnaissance, spanning multiple sectors and controller vendors.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA AA26-097A (updated 22 Jul 2026) / FBI / NSA / EPA / DOE / USCYBERCOM — via CISA & Industrial Cyber

items.title: Unit 42 chains three Siemens ROX II zero-days to root on industrial switches
items.content_text: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 disclosed a three-vulnerability exploit chain in Siemens ROX II operating-system switches — ruggedized devices used to route traffic inside substation, rail and plant networks. Chained together (CVE-2025-40948, -40947 and -40949, the last rated CVSS 9.1), an attacker moves from arbitrary file disclosure through a feature-key privilege-escalation flaw to full, persistent root access on the device. Individually the bugs range from medium to critical; the value of the write-up is showing how ordinary configuration and logic weaknesses compose into device takeover, and how a compromised OT switch becomes a durable pivot for lateral movement across the very network it segments. Siemens has published advisories (SSA-973901, -078743, -081142) and fixes in ROX II firmware V2.17.1.

items.title: July ICS Patch Tuesday: a CVSS 10 Siemens auth-bypass headlines a heavy month from the big three
items.content_text: Siemens, Rockwell Automation and Schneider Electric all shipped July advisories, and the volume matters as much as any single flaw. Siemens published nine advisories, six critical — including a CVSS 10 token-invalidation bug in Opcenter X that lets an attacker bypass authentication for full application access, plus critical fixes touching SIMATIC S7-1500, Mendix, Cadra and Desigo CC. Rockwell issued twelve advisories, two critical, one letting an unauthenticated attacker reach intrusive CLI commands on 1715 Redundant I/O. Schneider added an IGSS arbitrary-code-execution flaw and an EcoStruxure Cybersecurity Admin Expert authentication bypass. None are known to be exploited yet — but this gear sits at the core of energy, water and manufacturing plants, and the patch-to-exploit window keeps shrinking.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Siemens ProductCERT / Rockwell / Schneider PSIRT — via SecurityWeek

items.title: Siemens SICAM 8 grid-automation devices — DoS flaws and insecure OPC UA defaults
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-197-05 covers multiple vulnerabilities across Siemens SICAM 8 products, including SICAM A8000 and EGS device firmware used in substation automation and RTU roles. An HTTP-accessible debugging interface can let an authenticated attacker crash the web process for a denial-of-service condition (CVE-2026-54798 through -54801), and the affected application ships with a default configuration that disables all OPC UA security mechanisms — leaving that channel open to unauthorized access and control unless hardened. The advisory flags impact to the Energy and Critical Manufacturing sectors; Siemens directs customers to firmware V26.20 / V26.20.0 or later.

items.title: CISA flags Schneider Easergy protection relays and OpenPLC in early-July advisory batch
items.content_text: On 9 July CISA released three ICS advisories worth attention across energy and water. Schneider Electric’s Easergy MiCOM Px40 series protection relays — core to substation protection schemes — and Schneider’s PowerChute Serial Shutdown software were both flagged, alongside OpenPLC v3, the open-source PLC runtime used in water/wastewater and energy settings and increasingly common in labs and smaller utilities. Protection relays sit at the safety-critical layer of the grid, so relay firmware advisories deserve a fast read even when no exploitation is reported; OpenPLC deployments, often stood up outside formal asset management, are easy to overlook.

items.title: Hitachi Energy e-mesh EMS and PROMOD flagged in CISA’s 7 July advisories
items.content_text: CISA’s 7 July release of seven ICS advisories included two Hitachi Energy products — the e-mesh Energy Management System and PROMOD power-market simulation software — used by utilities for energy management and planning. The same batch covered Siemens Mendix Studio Pro and SINEC OS, Digi International PortServer TS and Digi One SP IA, a Hydro-Québec EV-charging backend, and Labcenter Proteus. Hitachi Energy products sit across generation, transmission and grid-edge operations, so its advisories tend to matter to power utilities even when severity varies — and they frequently reference third-party components that ripple into other vendors’ stacks.

items.title: Rockwell Logix controllers — CVSS 9.2 flaws force an unrecoverable fault, in CISA’s 16 July batch
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-197-06 covers denial-of-service flaws in Rockwell Automation CompactLogix, ControlLogix, Compact GuardLogix and GuardLogix controllers, with CISA assigning a CVSS 9.2 base score to the most severe entries (CVE-2025-12012 and CVE-2025-11698): an unauthenticated, low-complexity network attacker can write invalid file data and drive a controller into a major non-recoverable fault (MNRF) that requires on-site personnel to physically recover the device. A companion advisory (ICSA-26-197-08) flags a DoS issue in the Flex 5000 adapter. Rockwell began pushing firmware on 14 July. These are workhorse controllers on discrete and process floors, so an availability hit that halts a line or batch is a real operational event even without code execution.

items.title: CISA’s 23 July batch: Panduit IntraVUE lets an IT-side attacker reach control devices, plus Rockwell ThinManager, Weintek and Johnson Controls
items.content_text: CISA published seven fresh ICS advisories on 23 July (the ICSA-26-204 series) covering MZ Automation, Rockwell Automation, Panduit, Weintek and Johnson Controls — none known to be exploited, but several worth a scan. Panduit IntraVUE (ICSA-26-204-04, versions ≤3.2.1a14) stores passwords in plaintext, and CISA warns an attacker with IT-network access could manipulate connected industrial devices without physical access — exactly the IT-to-OT pivot defenders worry about. Weintek’s cMT3092X HMI (ICSA-26-204-03) lets a non-privileged user escalate rights or read other users’ credentials, and the batch adds Rockwell ThinManager (a widely deployed thin-client management server) and two Johnson Controls Metasys building-automation advisories. Small, IT-adjacent OT devices like these rarely make the asset inventory.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICSA-26-204-03 / -04 / -05 — via CISA & Patrick Coyle (Chemical Facility Security News)

items.title: CISA’s 28 July batch: Siemens SIMATIC S7-PLCSIM Advanced and Desigo CC among the ICSA-26-209 advisories
items.content_text: CISA published a fresh set of ICS advisories on 28 July (the ICSA-26-209 series). Two Siemens entries stand out: SIMATIC S7-PLCSIM Advanced (ICSA-26-209-03), where mishandling of high-volume multicast traffic can exhaust memory and let an unauthenticated attacker on the local network segment force a denial-of-service condition, and the Desigo CC building-management family (ICSA-26-209-01, versions V7, V8 and V9), affected by an OpenSSL stack-based buffer overflow that could cause a DoS or potentially remote code execution. The batch lands alongside a separate Rockwell Automation FactoryTalk Services Platform advisory (ICSA-26-202-07). None are reported as exploited, but PLC-simulation, building-management and FactoryTalk platform software sit close to engineering and plant operations, so they warrant an inventory cross-check.

items.title: CISA’s 30 July batch: eleven ICSA-26-211 advisories span Rockwell Logix comms modules, Siemens SIMATIC, Schneider IGSS and the MZ Automation IEC 60870 stack
items.content_text: CISA published eleven ICS advisories on 30 July (the ICSA-26-211 series). Among them, ICSA-26-211-05 covers a denial-of-service flaw in Rockwell Automation CompactLogix 5380, ControlLogix 5580 and the 1756-EN4TR communications module, where crafted traffic can knock the controller or adapter offline. ICSA-26-211-04 republishes Schneider Electric’s IGSS SCADA advisory, and other entries mirror Siemens SIMATIC ProductCERT notes and a vulnerability in MZ Automation’s lib60870 — an open-source IEC 60870-5 telecontrol library embedded in many utility RTU and gateway products. None are reported as exploited, but the comms-module and telecontrol-library items sit directly on grid and plant communication paths, so they warrant an inventory cross-check.

items.title: CISA and Five Eyes partners publish “CI Fortify” — pre-engineer OT isolation before an attack, not during one
items.content_text: On 28 July CISA, Australia’s ASD/ACSC, the UK NCSC, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and the FBI released joint guidance, “CI Fortify — Advice for Isolating Vital Systems,” giving critical-infrastructure operators practical steps to cut vital OT and enabling systems off from all other networks during a crisis and keep delivering the essential service in isolation for an extended period. The core message is that isolation has to be identified, engineered and rehearsed in advance: first define the minimum systems needed to keep the service running, then document every connection those systems have to corporate networks, remote access, cloud, internet-facing infrastructure, vendors and other operators, and build tested separation points you can actually invoke. Landing the same week as the Minnesota water incident (see top story), it is the defensive counterpart to that scenario — a ready-made framework for the manual-fallback and disconnect decisions those utilities had to make live.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA / ASD’s ACSC / UK NCSC / CCCS / FBI joint guidance — via CISA & BleepingComputer

items.title: NERC CIP-012-2 now in force — real-time data between control centers gets tighter protection
items.content_text: CIP-012-2 became effective 1 July 2026, strengthening requirements to protect real-time operational data exchanged between control centers against unauthorized disclosure, modification and loss of availability — closing gaps left by the earlier revision. It lands alongside CIP-003-9, whose enforcement began in April, which extends security-governance and vendor electronic-remote-access requirements into low-impact BES environments that historically saw minimal oversight. For registered entities the practical questions now are scope and evidence: which control-center links and low-impact assets are in play, and what documentation demonstrates compliance. Non-NERC operators can still borrow the intent — protect control-to-control communications and govern low-criticality remote access — as good practice.

items.title: OT Cyber Coalition pushes to make ISA/IEC 62443 the single global OT standard
items.content_text: The Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition released a position paper on 23 July urging US policymakers to formally recognize ISA/IEC 62443 as the global baseline for OT cybersecurity, arguing that an expanding patchwork of sector-specific mandates piles on compliance cost without improving real security. The paper points to the TSA’s pipeline security directives, NERC CIP’s “double-reporting” burden in the energy sector, and the EU’s overlapping NIS2, CER and Cyber Resilience Act requirements as cases where fragmented rules re-create controls already defined in 62443. For asset owners it is a useful signal of where harmonization pressure is building — and a reminder that a 62443-anchored program tends to map cleanly onto most of these regimes at once.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: OT Cybersecurity Coalition position paper — via Industrial Cyber
